power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: The case for a developmentally-informed education system in the early years

author.affiliation:
Faculty of Education
								Centre for Research on Play in Education Development and Learning (PEDAL)
								University of Cambridge
								
									UK

text.text: A developmentally-informed early years system is one that is underpinned by a clear understanding of children.
In this chapter we argue that this involves integrating scientific insights into child development with expertise in how public policy, services and practices can influence this development.

We present a framework of six core principles capturing essential knowledge about child development, which we propose should inform decisions about early childhood education and associated policies and services.
We explore these principles in the context of the Early Years landscape in England.
We consider challenges for this framework in the current system and explore what might be done to make the whole system -from front line practice to national policy -more developmentally-informed.
There are widespread reports that, post-COVID19 pandemic, increasing numbers of young children are arriving at school unprepared and lacking in basic skills needed to benefit from formal schooling.

In this chapter we argue that this situation underscores the necessity to position education in the earliest years of a child's life within a framework informed by the science of child development and delivered by practitioners who understand this science.
This chapter has two parts: First we explore what a developmentally-informed system might look like, describing universal principles which might be adopted and adapted in many places.

Second, we focus in on the English context and consider challenges in the current system and what might be done to make the whole system -from front line practice to national policy -more developmentally-informed.

In recent years, there has been increasing concern about the number of young children in the UK who are not ready for school, that is to say, they have not yet developed the basic skills they need to participate in learning in the reception year and beyond [Kindred Squared 2025].
text.formatted: In recent years, there has been increasing concern about the number of young children in the UK who are not ready for school, that is to say, they have not yet developed the basic skills they need to participate in learning in the reception year and beyond <ref type="bibr">[Kindred Squared 2025]</ref>.

text.text: Increasing levels of developmental delay and additional needs in four-and five-year-olds have been attributed to the lasting impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on babies, young children, their families and the services that work with them [Ofsted 2022].
text.formatted: Increasing levels of developmental delay and additional needs in four-and five-year-olds have been attributed to the lasting impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on babies, young children, their families and the services that work with them <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[Ofsted 2022</ref>].

text.text: Children starting school in 2024 and 2025 were the babies of lockdown, many of whom spent a vital period of their early development with limited social interactions, and in houses with increased stress and isolation.

Many services, such as health visiting, family support, and informal play groups, stopped or went online in lockdown and many have not fully returned to full face-to-face operation [Hogg and Mayes 2022].
text.formatted: Many services, such as health visiting, family support, and informal play groups, stopped or went online in lockdown and many have not fully returned to full face-to-face operation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[Hogg and Mayes 2022]</ref>.

text.text: The babies of the pandemic and their families are therefore doubly disadvantaged, facing the adversity of lockdown and without the support available to cohorts that preceded them [Ofsted 2022].
text.formatted: The babies of the pandemic and their families are therefore doubly disadvantaged, facing the adversity of lockdown and without the support available to cohorts that preceded them <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[Ofsted 2022</ref>].

text.text: The growth in developmental delays in the under-fives has also been attributed to other factors, such as cuts in public services, the cost-of-living crisis, increasing child poverty and the ubiquity of screens in family lives which disrupt healthy interactions and experiences [Nevin and Jacques 2024].
text.formatted: The growth in developmental delays in the under-fives has also been attributed to other factors, such as cuts in public services, the cost-of-living crisis, increasing child poverty and the ubiquity of screens in family lives which disrupt healthy interactions and experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[Nevin and Jacques 2024]</ref>.

text.text: Clearly, wide-ranging and asserted action is needed to ensure all our children are developing well in early childhood, with the support they need to thrive.

In this chapter, we argue that, to deliver better experiences and outcomes for the babies of the lockdown era -and indeed all children -our education system must be developmentally-informed, which is not always the case at present.

At its most basic, a developmentally-informed system is one that is underpinned by a clear understanding of children, how they develop, and how public policy and services can influence this development.

It is one where decision-makers at all levels, from policy to practice, have a clear understanding of the biological, psychological and social processes that influence child development, and where an understanding of child development (amongst other considerations) informs their decisions.
A developmentally-informed system is a child-centred system, where children are well understood and their needs guide the work of the professionals and services around them.

Human developmental science is the study of the processes and mechanisms of stability and change over time [Petersen 2024] and in this chapter we narrow the scope to the early childhood period of 0-5 years.
text.formatted: Human developmental science is the study of the processes and mechanisms of stability and change over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[Petersen 2024]</ref> and in this chapter we narrow the scope to the early childhood period of 0-5 years.

text.text: Later in this chapter we outline six core principles of child development which a developmentally-informed system should acknowledge and act upon.
In advocating for the science of child development to inform early education, we are not aligning with any particular theoretical account.
Indeed, we take the view that different theories of human development can bring different perspectives that help elucidate aspects of a child's life in important ways [Newman and Newman 2022].
text.formatted: Indeed, we take the view that different theories of human development can bring different perspectives that help elucidate aspects of a child's life in important ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[Newman and Newman 2022]</ref>.

text.text: Understanding human development is particularly pertinent in early childhood (the period from birth until age 5).
We believe that being developmentally-informed is an important component of quality in services during this period.
It is widely recognised that the earliest years of life are a vital period in development, which lay the foundations for lifelong health and wellbeing.

During this period of rapid development, babies and young children's brains are shaped by their experiences, environments and interactions with the people around them [National Scientific Council on the Developing Child 2004].
Brain plasticity is greatest in the earliest years of life, so this is a prime time to support children's learning and development.

It is easier to shape neural connections and circuits as they are forming, rather than to modify them once they have matured [Hambrick et al. 2019; National Scientific Council on the Developing Child 2007].
text.formatted: It is easier to shape neural connections and circuits as they are forming, rather than to modify them once they have matured <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[Hambrick et al. 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">National Scientific Council on the Developing Child 2007]</ref>.

text.text: Experiences in early childhood play a particularly important role in shaping children's lives and life chances: positive early experiences can set children on a positive developmental trajectory, better able to seize opportunities ahead of them and to thrive.

Positive experiences and positive relationships with adults in early childhood have been linked to a wide range of outcomes throughout the life course, underpinning our mental and physical health, our learning and earning, and our ability to form positive relationships and contribute to society [National Scientific Council on the Developing Child 2004].
text.formatted: Positive experiences and positive relationships with adults in early childhood have been linked to a wide range of outcomes throughout the life course, underpinning our mental and physical health, our learning and earning, and our ability to form positive relationships and contribute to society <ref type="bibr">[National Scientific Council on the Developing Child 2004]</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, because development in early childhood is the foundation for later development, disruptions in early development can have a disproportionate impact on children's wellbeing and development, leading to a child being more susceptible to poor outcomes throughout their lives [Hambrick et al. 2019].
text.formatted: In contrast, because development in early childhood is the foundation for later development, disruptions in early development can have a disproportionate impact on children's wellbeing and development, leading to a child being more susceptible to poor outcomes throughout their lives <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[Hambrick et al. 2019]</ref>.

text.text: Early experiences do not determine our later outcomes, but their ripples can be felt throughout our lives, for better or worse.
Alongside being an important stage in development, early childhood is also qualitatively different from other life stages (and indeed in itself consists of several different stages).
Babies and young children are not just smaller versions of older children.
Their needs and abilities are fundamentally different, and this must inform how we develop services and policies to support them.
This is particularly true of the youngest babies, who are non-verbal and totally dependent on adults for their care [Winnicott 2018].
text.formatted: This is particularly true of the youngest babies, who are non-verbal and totally dependent on adults for their care <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[Winnicott 2018</ref>].

text.text: Current policy changes also make it pertinent to consider the earliest years of education.

Thanks to policy and funding changes in recent decades, and because more children now grow up in families where both parents are in paid employment, more children are in formal early education and childcare.
In England, more than 90% of children are in formal early education and childcare before they start school [Department for Education 2025].
As time goes by there is a clear trend: more children are accessing early education for more of their young lives.
Children are also starting early education and childcare at an earlier age.
In 2025, the age at which families are entitled to Government subsidised early education and childcare in England is lowering to nine-months old.
Babies are more reliant on the adults around them compared to older children, and their brains are more malleable and influenced by experience .
Therefore, the quality of early education and childcare matters even more at this age [Sylva et al. 2011].
text.formatted: Therefore, the quality of early education and childcare matters even more at this age <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[Sylva et al. 2011]</ref>.

text.text: We have developed a framework of six core principles (see list below), which we believe capture essential knowledge about child development that should inform decisions about early childhood education and associated policies and services.
These principles are inter-related and overlapping.
They are based on our own expert judgement, reading of the academic and grey literature, and many years working in the system.
This framework has not been described in this way before and would benefit from being tested and refined in practice and research.
(1) First things First.
In the first years of life, children acquire skills and abilities that form the foundations of later learning and development.
(2) Always Changing.
Development is dynamic, complex and not deterministic.
(3) Relationships Matter.
Relationships are perhaps the most influential factor in early development.
These six principles provide a framework for understanding early childhood development.

Such a framework does not negate the need for specific knowledge informed by, say, the latest insights from cognitive science or domain specific knowledge such as typical language development or executive functioning trajectories.

Rather, the principles are intended as a broader context that will support practitioners and others to understand how such specific knowledge 'fits in' to the broader learning and development journey of each child.
We now explain each principle in more depth.
First things First -The importance of foundational learning.
Children develop in a particular way -they develop core foundational skills early in childhood, which then support the development of more specific and sophisticated knowledge and skills.
For example, a child must develop the ability to focus their attention, and must have some basic language skills, before they can learn to read.
Skills such as the ability to focus thoughts, to communicate, and to regulate oneself are vital foundations on which other learning and development is built.
Practitioners and policy makers may focus on particular aspects of early development, such as 'language development', 'motor skills' and 'mathematics'.
But knowledge of child development shows that these domains are not as distinct as sometimes imagined.

They have common developmental pathways and are mutually influential -for example language development is influenced by and influences emotional regulation, motor development, mathematical competence and so on [Adolph and Hoch 2019; Kuzik et al. 2020; Turan and De Smedt 2023].
text.formatted: They have common developmental pathways and are mutually influential -for example language development is influenced by and influences emotional regulation, motor development, mathematical competence and so on <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[Adolph and Hoch 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kuzik et al. 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Turan and De Smedt 2023]</ref>.

text.text: Because of the foundational nature of early skills, perturbations to the complex web of inputs to the developmental system in the early years can have outsized impacts compared to similar disruptions experienced by those in different developmental periods [Dunn et al. 2017; Hambrick et al. 2019].
text.formatted: Because of the foundational nature of early skills, perturbations to the complex web of inputs to the developmental system in the early years can have outsized impacts compared to similar disruptions experienced by those in different developmental periods <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[Dunn et al. 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hambrick et al. 2019</ref>].

text.text: This may be why children who were babies and young children during the pandemic experience more pervasive and lasting effects than those who were older.
One implication of this principle is that, to ensure good outcomes in childhood and later, it is important to support the development of foundational skills in early childhood.
Developmentally-informed practice recognises the importance of foundational learning and development, and how it underpins the acquisition of academic knowledge and technical skills.

This leads to a confidence, for example, in supporting children to learn through play rather than rushing to learn explicit phonics, literacy or numeracy too young-knowing that the skills and development acquired through positive play experiences will provide strong foundations on which more academic learning will build, when the time is right.
For example, pretend play can support children's social and linguistic skills, which are important for later literacy [Gibson et al. 2020 [Gibson et al. , 2021]].
text.formatted: For example, pretend play can support children's social and linguistic skills, which are important for later literacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[Gibson et al. 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[Gibson et al. , 2021]]</ref>.

text.text: Another implication is that children who have experienced adversity or lacked the opportunities to develop foundational skills in early childhood will need support to develop these skills first before they can meaningfully acquire other skills.

Importantly, a developmentally-informed perspective here does not align with a simple 'catch up' model, even if we were to 'hot house' reception aged children to teach them skills valued in the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) (e.g. holding a pencil correctly or recognising phonics) we would not fully compensate for the missed early life experiences that would typically underpin the emergence of such skills.
Child development is a highly complex, nonlinear, process of change.
Development happens as the result of a vast array of interacting biological, psychological, environmental, relational and societal factors.

At any given point in time, a child's current developmental state (or profile) will be a consequence of these interactions and of their preceding developmental state and trajectory [Karmiloff-Smith 2009].
text.formatted: At any given point in time, a child's current developmental state (or profile) will be a consequence of these interactions and of their preceding developmental state and trajectory <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[Karmiloff-Smith 2009]</ref>.

text.text: To paraphrase Heckman, the science of child development shows us that the 'nature vs nurture' debate is no longer relevant [Heckman 2008].
text.formatted: To paraphrase Heckman, the science of child development shows us that the 'nature vs nurture' debate is no longer relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[Heckman 2008]</ref>.

text.text: A child's nature and their experiences shape each other.
For example, a child whose temperament leads them to be more irritable, and to react more quickly and intensely to negative experiences will influence how the adults around them act towards them.
This child will also experience and respond to the same adult behaviours differently to a child with lower reactivity and a calmer temperament.
Every individual child both shapes and experiences their environment differently [Bates et al. 2012].
text.formatted: Every individual child both shapes and experiences their environment differently <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[Bates et al. 2012</ref>].

text.text: Our understanding of child development has been transformed by research showing that when experiencing the same types of adversity, some children show more susceptibility than others to adverse outcomes [Moffitt et al. 2006; Zhang et al. 2023].
text.formatted: Our understanding of child development has been transformed by research showing that when experiencing the same types of adversity, some children show more susceptibility than others to adverse outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[Moffitt et al. 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Zhang et al. 2023]</ref>.

text.text: Factors protecting against adverse outcomes include biological factors, positive relationships, high-quality early education, economic stability, parental harmony, diverse social relationships, community cohesion and resources, belonging within a religious or cultural community, participation in arts and cultural activities like sports or dance, and so on [Schoon et al. 2004; Vanderbilt-Adriance and Shaw 2008].
text.formatted: Factors protecting against adverse outcomes include biological factors, positive relationships, high-quality early education, economic stability, parental harmony, diverse social relationships, community cohesion and resources, belonging within a religious or cultural community, participation in arts and cultural activities like sports or dance, and so on <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[Schoon et al. 2004</ref>; Vanderbilt-Adriance and <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Shaw 2008]</ref>.

text.text: Because of the complexity of early childhood development.
Outcomes in early childhood are therefore not deterministic but probabilistic.
Any particular input or combination of inputs rarely determines a particular outcome but simply increases or decreases the risk of it occurring.
For instance, nurturing care and good early relationships make it more likely a child will thrive, while adversity may increase the risk of difficulties.
There is always the opportunity to influence a child's developmental trajectory through increasing protective factors and addressing risks.

Whilst the existence of one particular risk factor does not determine poor outcomes, the accumulation of risk factors increases the probability of poor outcomes substantially, as does the depth and persistence of adversity.

A child experiencing a temporary period of poverty, for example, may only have a small risk of poor outcomes, whereas a child experiencing deep and persistent poverty, alongside factors such as parental stress, poor housing, and exposure to conflict and abuse, will be at heightened risk of a range of poor outcomes [Felitti et al. 1998; Rutter 1979].

text.text: The implication of this dynamic complexity is that educators must be able to recognise and respond to the different needs and experiences of different children, and systems must support this.
In the example above, we described how pretend play can support the development of a range of skills.

However, the implication of this second principle is that the developmental 'gain' associated with such a play episode would depend on many factors about the child and their circumstances, such as whether the child had previously experience of socialising with other children, whether they are tired, hungry or feeling unsafe, whether they have a caregiver who is able to support and scaffold their play experiences, and so on.
This shows us that early childhood education can never be a one-size fits all endeavour.
Practitioners must be skilled in fine-tuning education to each child's individual characteristics, experiences and context.
They must also be curious about each child understanding that the same profile may emerge in children for different reasons [Cicchetti and Rogosch 1996].
text.formatted: They must also be curious about each child understanding that the same profile may emerge in children for different reasons <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[Cicchetti and Rogosch 1996]</ref>.

text.text: For example, language delay may be due to physiological or neurological issues, wider developmental delay, or early neglect and adversity.
To support a child's development, a practitioner consider the factors that have influenced their development and therefore the most appropriate response to any challenges [Shaw et al. 2024].
text.formatted: To support a child's development, a practitioner consider the factors that have influenced their development and therefore the most appropriate response to any challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[Shaw et al. 2024]</ref>.

text.text: At a systems level, early education systems must enable practitioners to gain a deep understanding of an individual child (for example, by enabling continuity of care, supporting home-school relationships, and facilitating information sharing between services).

In recognition of the cumulative impact of risk, additional support and targeted provision should respond to patterns of risk factors in children and families rather than a binary response to individual risks.
Relationships Matter -Relationships are the essence of survival and flourishing.
Developmental science has also shown us the central importance of relationships to young children's development [Sroufe 2000].
text.formatted: Developmental science has also shown us the central importance of relationships to young children's development <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[Sroufe 2000</ref>].

text.text: From an evolutionary perspective the relational aspect of the extended period of immaturity experienced by humans has been proposed as essential for the development of advanced environmental adaptability [Sander 1975].
text.formatted: From an evolutionary perspective the relational aspect of the extended period of immaturity experienced by humans has been proposed as essential for the development of advanced environmental adaptability <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[Sander 1975]</ref>.

text.text: Bonds between parent and child are essential for immediate and long-term survival and flourishing.
Beyond immediate survival, nurturing adult-child relationships support a wide range of developmental pathways.
For example, an adult's attunement to a child matters, for their learning of self-and co-regulation, and of the motivation and intentions of others [Stern 1985].
text.formatted: For example, an adult's attunement to a child matters, for their learning of self-and co-regulation, and of the motivation and intentions of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[Stern 1985</ref>].

text.text: Adults' attunement, and the extent to which they follow and respond to child's cues and attention has been linked to a range of later outcomes, including language learning and vocabulary [Tamis-LeMonda et al. 2019; Tomasello and Farrar 1986].
text.formatted: Adults' attunement, and the extent to which they follow and respond to child's cues and attention has been linked to a range of later outcomes, including language learning and vocabulary <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[Tamis-LeMonda et al. 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Tomasello and Farrar 1986]</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, research grounded in attachment theory has shown how early relationships underpin the development of emotional and social functioning, as well as the development of cognitive skills such as working memory, and inhibitory and attentional control [Bernier et al. 2010; Ding et al. 2014].

text.text: The impact of adult-child relationships is not just about parents.
Research in the US has found that extended family can be important for supporting child development [Jæger 2012], with effects varying across different ethnic groups [Mollborn et al. 2011].
text.formatted: Research in the US has found that extended family can be important for supporting child development <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[Jæger 2012]</ref>, with effects varying across different ethnic groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[Mollborn et al. 2011]</ref>.

text.text: Beyond family relationships, strong educator-child relationship quality is linked to positive developmental gains at preschool, showing that the underlying relational principle is important across caregiver roles and types [Pianta and Stuhlman 2004; Verschueren and Koomen 2012].
text.formatted: Beyond family relationships, strong educator-child relationship quality is linked to positive developmental gains at preschool, showing that the underlying relational principle is important across caregiver roles and types <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[Pianta and Stuhlman 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Verschueren and Koomen 2012]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, opportunities for relational engagement with other children, whether siblings, extended family or peers, support young children's learning.

Research into peer effects is relatively underdeveloped in comparison to adult-child relationships but peers have been shown to influence language development [Mashburn et al. 2009], social-emotional development [Zhao and Gibson 2023], academic attainment [Hanushek et al. 2003; Neidell and Waldfogel 2010] and school readiness [Delay et al. 2015].

text.text: The implications of this third principle include the importance of nurturing responsive relationships in early education settings, both between early educators and children, and between children and their peers.

In addition, early educators must be alert to a child's early relational experiences and how these may have shaped their development: children arriving in early education having experienced relational adversity are likely to need additional support.

A developmentally-informed education system must recognise that the biggest influences on a child's educational outcomes lie outside the education system -not only in children's early relationships, but also in their wider environments and experiences.

In recent years in the UK, there has been a drive for more trauma-informed practice, with practitioners across the workforce trained to understand more about the impacts of trauma and adverse child experiences, on development, wellbeing and behaviours.

This increased understanding is welcome, but trauma is only one part of the complex array of factors that shape us in early life, and indeed the impacts of trauma on humans can vary [Hambrick et al. 2019].
text.formatted: This increased understanding is welcome, but trauma is only one part of the complex array of factors that shape us in early life, and indeed the impacts of trauma on humans can vary <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[Hambrick et al. 2019]</ref>.

text.text: A developmentally-informed system moves us beyond being simply trauma-informed, to develop understanding and responses to all of the factors which may have shaped development.
Children's life circumstances and socio-cultural contexts are highly impactful upon their learning and growth [Shonkoff and Phillips 2000].
text.formatted: Children's life circumstances and socio-cultural contexts are highly impactful upon their learning and growth <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[Shonkoff and Phillips 2000]</ref>.

text.text: Research shows, for example, that both parent-child relationships and the activities and resources allocated to children's learning by their families can have a lasting educational impact [Parker et al. 1999; Rose et al. 2018; Tamis-LeMonda et al. 2019].
text.formatted: Research shows, for example, that both parent-child relationships and the activities and resources allocated to children's learning by their families can have a lasting educational impact <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[Parker et al. 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Rose et al. 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tamis-LeMonda et al. 2019]</ref>.

text.text: The time and resource a family can devote to their child's development is highly influenced by their economic and social resources [Conger and Donnellan 2007; Masarik and Conger 2017].

text.text: Furthermore, growing up in economically deprived neighbourhoods can also have a lasting impact upon child development, above and beyond effects explained by immediate family circumstances [Aikens and Barbarin 2008; Oliver et al. 2007; Wodtke et al. 2011].

text.text: These effects exert influence in different ways, for example via the quantity, quality and coordination of local services or the quality, safety and availability of local cultural assets like parks and museums [Aikens and Barbarin 2008].

text.text: Beyond economic and physical circumstances and contexts, cultural values, beliefs and experiences also impact upon the developing child.

For example, motor milestones such as age of sitting and walking or the presence of a crawling stage vary according to cultural child rearing practices such as supine sleeping or infant massage [Karasik et al. 2010].

text.text: The implications of this fourth principle are that educators must be alert to a child's family, culture, community and economic position and the impact these might have on their needs and abilities.

A system that aims to support children to reach their full potential, cannot focus only on what happens in the education institutions but must look to influence the broader societal systems which support our children to learn and grow.
Outcomes-and mission-focused approaches, which integrate the design and delivery of education into a wider policy agenda could leverage change at this systemic level.
As well as understanding contexts and processes of development, it is also essential that we understand children at an individual level.

While 'staged' models of child development have an intuitive appeal, and checklists for developmental milestones are popular, decades of developmental science have shown that child development is characterised by high levels of variability, even amongst children of similar ages and backgrounds.
There is also substantial within child variability.
Children's developmental competences can vary by situation and across different aspects of development.
For example, a child may demonstrate confidence, independence and strong language development at home, but may be reserved, quiet and unforthcoming in a nursery setting.

Note that we are not claiming there are no developmental generalisations to be made, but rather that recognising and understanding individual variability is key to an understanding of children and how to support their learning [Pérez-Edgar et al. 2020].
text.formatted: Note that we are not claiming there are no developmental generalisations to be made, but rather that recognising and understanding individual variability is key to an understanding of children and how to support their learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[Pérez-Edgar et al. 2020]</ref>.

text.text: We further argue, in line with a neurodiversity-based perspective, that developmental variability is a desirable characteristic of human populations.

Understanding this is especially important for young children displaying initial signs of neurodivergence where environmental and cognitive factors mean that careful appreciation of and adjustment to their needs and profile by caregivers and educators is essential to wellbeing, learning and participation [Gibson and McNally 2024].

text.text: Being and becoming -The importance of children's rights, perspectives and agency.
The final tenet of developmentally-informed early childhood education is that children play an active role in their own learning and development.

Social constructivist approaches [Vygotsky 1978] propose that children bring their own experiences, interests, and prior knowledge to education, which shape how they engage with and construct new understanding.
text.formatted: Social constructivist approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[Vygotsky 1978]</ref> propose that children bring their own experiences, interests, and prior knowledge to education, which shape how they engage with and construct new understanding.

text.text: Given the huge number of external influences and maturational processes at play in early childhood development, this factor is sometimes overlooked but it has important implications for how we conceptualise and enact early learning.

One intriguing finding to support this view is that children have been shown to learn words more readily when they belong to categories that they are interested in [Ackermann et al. 2020] -for example, a child preferring animals to vehicles might learn the words lion, elephant and capybara more quickly than ambulance, tank or hovercraft.
text.formatted: One intriguing finding to support this view is that children have been shown to learn words more readily when they belong to categories that they are interested in <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Ackermann et al. 2020]</ref> -for example, a child preferring animals to vehicles might learn the words lion, elephant and capybara more quickly than ambulance, tank or hovercraft.

text.text: Linked to this, it is also important that education systems recognise the rights of babies and young children, and the importance of their views and interests being taken into account.

Education systems can sometimes be so focussed on end goals -on the production of competent, skilled, engaged young adults -that the subjective experiences, perspectives and rights of children at every stage of the system are overlooked.

This is particularly true in early childhood, where a focus on improving outcomes often takes priority over a focus on the in-the-moment experiences of babies and young children, and it can be assumed that, because they are often non-verbal, young children do not have a voice that needs to be considered in decision making.
In fact, from birth babies are able to communicate their preferences and interests -if only adults take the time to tune in and notice these non-verbal cues.
Babies and young children thrive when the adults around them notice and respond to their preferences and needs.

In a multitude of ways, babies and young children are able to voice their own opinions about what supports their learning and development and this too can and should shape educational experiences [O'Farrelly et al. 2020].
text.formatted: In a multitude of ways, babies and young children are able to voice their own opinions about what supports their learning and development and this too can and should shape educational experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[O'Farrelly et al. 2020]</ref>.

text.text: When putting these principles to work in the design of early childhood services and settings, it is important that decision makers take a full view of the variability within the early childhood period, ensuring the needs of different age groups and profiles are taken into account.

In previous work, we have highlighted instances where policy makers, local commissioners and service managers have not taken the specific developmental needs of the youngest children into account and where babies and young children have been systematically excluded from benefiting from policies or services.
These include the lockdown rules in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, where, as lockdown eased, there were rules which only enabled each of us to meet only one other person.
For many months, these applied to all children too.
Given that young children cannot go out without a parent, this meant they were not able to see friends or family members.

Another example is that child mental health services nominally commissioned for from 0-18 years often have none of the expertise to support babies and young children and have inclusion criteria that often explicitly or implicitly excludes babies and young children [Hogg 2019].
text.formatted: Another example is that child mental health services nominally commissioned for from 0-18 years often have none of the expertise to support babies and young children and have inclusion criteria that often explicitly or implicitly excludes babies and young children <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[Hogg 2019</ref>].

text.text: Arguably at present, dominant voices in the early childhood sector do not promote developmentally appropriate expectations of children.

A 2025 report on school readiness in England, for example, reported a 'problem' that -according to a survey of over 1000 reception teachers in 2024, 45% of children are unable to sit still [Kindred Squared 2025, p.7.].
text.formatted: A 2025 report on school readiness in England, for example, reported a 'problem' that -according to a survey of over 1000 reception teachers in 2024, 45% of children are unable to sit still <ref type="bibr">[Kindred Squared 2025, p.7.]</ref>.

text.text: This is, we argue, an example of a system that is not developmentally-informed: very few children of that age could be reasonably expected to sit still for any length of time.
This example is illustrative of the conflation of school readiness and a good level of development in the English early education system.

Discussions about the development of our four-and five-year-olds, are often not about whether children are showing a healthy level of development, but more about whether they are demonstrating a specific set of behaviours that ensure classroom compliance.
As an aside, this might, perhaps, be why so many boys fall behind in measures of school readiness and early development, compared to girls.
Sixty-one percent of boys in England in 2024 were recorded as having a good level of development at the end of reception, compared to 75% of girls [Department for Education 2024].

Maybe many boys are demonstrating the levels of health and development that would be expected at their age, but they are less likely to behave in ways which are valued in the classroom (such as sitting still, playing quietly).

School readiness scores might be more equal if our teachers had developmentally appropriate expectations of boys and understood what healthy development looks like for different children at different points in their developmental journey.

It is widely agreed that decision makers, both in policy and practice, should be informed by evidence, which can help them make the best choices for babies, children and families, in order to improve outcomes, make good use of resources, and avoid harm [Pampaka et al. 2016; Styles and Torgerson 2018].

text.text: There has, however, in children's policy, been a narrow understanding of what it means to be evidence-informed.
In recent decades UK policy discourse -including in early childhood -has been influenced significantly by a 'what works' agenda [Foundations 2025; Pampaka et al. 2016].
text.formatted: In recent decades UK policy discourse -including in early childhood -has been influenced significantly by a 'what works' agenda <ref type="bibr">[Foundations 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Pampaka et al. 2016]</ref>.

text.text: From classroom practice through to national policy, decision makers are increasingly expected to draw upon high-quality, research-based evidence about which interventions make most difference when selecting actions to make a positive impact in their sphere of influence.

Traditionally, this emphasis on evidence-based practice has tended to focus on interventions that can be implemented and tested within a randomised controlled trial, with clearly defined control and intervention groups, a readily manipulated independent variable and a clear outcome measure.
Applying the developmental principles outlined above also helps to show the limitations of Randomised Control Trials (RCTs) and other quasi-experimental evidence about the impact of interventions.
Every child is an individual, and each one shaped in their own unique and complex way to the factors in their environment, experiences and relationships.
Therefore, while useful, RCT evidence must be interpreted with care: What works in one context, or for one child, for example, therefore may not work for others.
RCT evidence may tell decision makers that an intervention worked in a particular time and place, but that does not necessarily mean it will work in their community in future.
It would be difficult for any decision maker to select interventions and navigate research evidence, without also having a good knowledge of child development.
Without being developmentally-informed, how do decision makers identify where variations in children's outcomes are of concern, and where they reflect expected variation?
How do they understand which outcomes interventions should be influencing at which stages of development in order to change children's developmental trajectories and later outcomes?
Furthermore, to deliver high-quality services, early educators need to know more than simply how to deliver specific interventions.
We wouldn't think someone was a good mechanic if they could only change a tyre or refill a fuel tank -we expect mechanics to know how engines work, and how to make them work better.

Similarly, an early educator must not only understand a techniques and strategies for educating children, but should also have a deep understanding of how children 'work' -that is, their development and how it can be supported.
This is not to say that evidence about the impact of interventions is not useful.
Rather that it should not be used to support the 'lift and shift' of interventions from one community to another, with the assumption that they will be as effective.

A broader conceptualisation of evidence-informed practice [Nelson and Campbell 2017], emphasises how the impact of interventions provides a tool for decision makers, which, together with their own expertise (including an understanding of child development) and their knowledge of the child, family and community in front of them, can support them to make good decisions.
text.formatted: A broader conceptualisation of evidence-informed practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[Nelson and Campbell 2017]</ref>, emphasises how the impact of interventions provides a tool for decision makers, which, together with their own expertise (including an understanding of child development) and their knowledge of the child, family and community in front of them, can support them to make good decisions.

text.text: In short, we must broaden our understanding of what it means to be evidence-informed, to include being informed by evidence of child development, as well as by evidence of interventions and their impact.

Given that early development is so important, and can be shaped by children's environments and experiences, early childhood presents an opportunity when well-designed interventions and high-quality services can change a child's developmental trajectory, influencing their life and life chances.

A wide range of services can have contact with babies, children and families during this time, including early childhood education and care, but also maternity, health visiting and wider health, education and family support services delivered by both the public, private and voluntary sectors.
Research clearly demonstrates what is intuitively obvious: It is not enough simply to offer services to babies and young children, the quality of services matters.
Quality determines the extent to which any service or intervention can deliver its desired results.
Good quality care can improve outcomes for children, whilst exposure to poor quality services can harm child development [Sylva et al. 2011].
text.formatted: Good quality care can improve outcomes for children, whilst exposure to poor quality services can harm child development <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[Sylva et al. 2011</ref>].

text.text: In early childhood education and care, the quality of the workforce makes a significant impact on children's wellbeing, enjoyment and outcomes.

A wealth of evidence demonstrates that a more highly educated, well-trained workforce is associated with higher quality provision and better outcomes for children both in the early years and later at school [Burchinal et al. 2002; Gambaro 2017].
text.formatted: A wealth of evidence demonstrates that a more highly educated, well-trained workforce is associated with higher quality provision and better outcomes for children both in the early years and later at school <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[Burchinal et al. 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gambaro 2017]</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly important for children from more disadvantaged backgrounds or minoritised communities, and those with additional needs [Pascal et al. 2020].
text.formatted: This is particularly important for children from more disadvantaged backgrounds or minoritised communities, and those with additional needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[Pascal et al. 2020]</ref>.

text.text: It is therefore vital to ensure that practitioners have a good understanding of early childhood development, have developmentally appropriate expectations of children, and can tailor their approaches for the children they work with.
This is not a new argument.

In her 2012 review of the early years workforce Cathy Nutbrown put understanding of child development as her first priority in her list of what we should expect of practitioners with childcare and early education qualifications [Nutbrown 2012].

text.text: Sadly however, despite the acknowledgement of the importance of good knowledge of child development, this is often lacking.
This is part of a broader challenge relating to quality in the workforce, which has been an issue not only in England, but in many countries for many years [Gambaro 2017].
text.formatted: This is part of a broader challenge relating to quality in the workforce, which has been an issue not only in England, but in many countries for many years <ref type="bibr">[Gambaro 2017]</ref>.

text.text: Levels of training and qualification can be low.
Low pay and demanding conditions make it hard to recruit and retain talented staff and to incentivise professional development [Pascal et al. 2020].
text.formatted: Low pay and demanding conditions make it hard to recruit and retain talented staff and to incentivise professional development <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[Pascal et al. 2020]</ref>.

text.text: Even if practitioners are trained, large group sizes and scarce resources may make it difficult for them to implement what they have learned [Gambaro 2017].
text.formatted: Even if practitioners are trained, large group sizes and scarce resources may make it difficult for them to implement what they have learned <ref type="bibr">[Gambaro 2017</ref>].

text.text: The quality of the early education and childcare profession is varied.
There are many routes into the early years workforce, and to develop once in the workforce.
The nature, quality and content of early educators' training and development programmes vary hugely [Education Endowment Foundation 2025].
text.formatted: The nature, quality and content of early educators' training and development programmes vary hugely <ref type="bibr">[Education Endowment Foundation 2025]</ref>.

text.text: There are many exemplary professionals, but there are also widespread gaps in knowledge, competencies and skills.
These include gaps in knowledge about child development.
Very few training and development programmes seem to consistently provide a good grounding in developmental science [Campbell-Barr et al. 2020; Pascal et al. 2020].
text.formatted: Very few training and development programmes seem to consistently provide a good grounding in developmental science <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[Campbell-Barr et al. 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Pascal et al. 2020]</ref>.

text.text: Analysis of the content covered in university-level early childhood programmes showed that just over half of the degrees reviewed referenced content on child development [Education Endowment Foundation 2025].
text.formatted: Analysis of the content covered in university-level early childhood programmes showed that just over half of the degrees reviewed referenced content on child development <ref type="bibr">[Education Endowment Foundation 2025]</ref>.

text.text: To create a developmentally-informed system, it will be vital to ensure that all early educators and allied professionals have high-quality training in child development, as described by Nutbrown above.
As we described at the start of this chapter, in a developmentally-informed system decision-makers at all levels, from policy to practice, would be informed by an understanding of child development.
This is, therefore, not just about early educators or other service providers, but also about national and local decision makers having a clear understanding of early development.

To design policies, interventions or services that will work, decision-makers need at least a basic understanding of which children are at risk of poor outcomes, the developmental pathways that lead to different outcomes, and the mechanisms through which interventions can produce change [Olds and Kitzman 1993].
text.formatted: To design policies, interventions or services that will work, decision-makers need at least a basic understanding of which children are at risk of poor outcomes, the developmental pathways that lead to different outcomes, and the mechanisms through which interventions can produce change <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[Olds and Kitzman 1993]</ref>.

text.text: The system in England is not currently configured to support this; Civil Servants in the UK Government, for example, often move around policy areas and come to post without deep expertise in the specific areas of policy they work on and the underpinning science.
They are usually expected to be generalists -able to work across a broad range of policy areas and regularly move between them.

Professional development in the Civil Service tends to focus on the generic skills required to perform a broad function, such as policy development, not on enhancing understanding relating to an area of public service delivery, such as child development or education [Croxford and Hogg 2024].
text.formatted: Professional development in the Civil Service tends to focus on the generic skills required to perform a broad function, such as policy development, not on enhancing understanding relating to an area of public service delivery, such as child development or education <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[Croxford and Hogg 2024]</ref>.

text.text: Improving policy makers' understanding of child development feels critical to enable national and local decision makers to make informed decisions about where to invest or how to configure and commission services.
At the University of Cambridge, we ran a small programme to enable policy makers to learn more about early child development, with positive impacts on their work [Croxford and Hogg 2024].
text.formatted: At the University of Cambridge, we ran a small programme to enable policy makers to learn more about early child development, with positive impacts on their work <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[Croxford and Hogg 2024]</ref>.

text.text: Such programmes might be developed as a routine part of civil servant's professional development.
So, to end, how do we create a developmentally-informed system?

Our goal should be to work towards a system where practitioners and decision-makers have a clear understanding of the biological, psychological and social processes that influence child development, and where an understanding of child development informs their decisions.
A developmentally-informed system is a child-centred system, where children are well understood and their needs guide the work of the professionals and services around them.

Part of the solution is about training, ensuring all early childhood education and care practitioners have a good grounding of early child development in their pre-qualification training and ongoing professional development, and ensuring others in the system -including commissioners and policy makers at a local and national level -also have opportunities to develop this knowledge.

But change is about more than professional development and training, it is about looking at the values and principles which inform and shape how systems work: what is valued and rewarded in commissioning decisions, funding and performance management systems, and accountability frameworks?
What is the focus of management discussions and supervision?

Creating a developmentally-informed system requires system change -creating, over a time, a child-centred system, where children are well understood and their needs consistently guide the work of the professionals and services around them.
The profound educational impacts of the pandemic lockdowns on babies and young children demonstrate that the foundations of learning lie in the earliest years of life.

We have set out a rationale for a new approach to the early years education system that takes into account the cumulative body of evidence about the processes of learning and development at this crucial life stage.
We advocate for a developmentally-informed model, and for freeing the concept of education from schools, settings or curricula.

We set out six core principles that underly a developmentally-informed approach, together with practical examples of how these principles might inform the actions of different stakeholders in an educational system.
We hope that research, policy and practice communities will be inspired to apply these principles to their work.
